questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Conditions that make Rolle's theorem apply
questions.learningObjective: state the three hypotheses Rolle's theorem needs before its conclusion is guaranteed
questions.stem: Rolle's theorem is stated for a function on a closed interval. Which group of three conditions must hold before the conclusion that the derivative vanishes somewhere inside is guaranteed?

options.text: f is continuous on the closed interval, differentiable on the open interval, and takes equal values at the two endpoints
f is continuous on the open interval, differentiable on the closed interval, and takes equal values at the two endpoints
options.misconception: swaps the intervals, asking for differentiability at the closed endpoints instead of in the open interior

options.text: f is continuous on the closed interval, differentiable on the open interval, and takes a smaller value at the left endpoint
options.misconception: thinks the theorem needs the endpoint values to be unequal rather than equal

options.text: f is continuous on the open interval, differentiable on the open interval, and takes equal values at the two endpoints
options.misconception: believes continuity on the closed interval is unnecessary, that the interior alone is enough

questions.explanation: All three conditions are load bearing. Continuity on the closed interval lets the extreme value theorem hand back an absolute maximum and minimum that are actually attained, including at the endpoints. Differentiability on the open interior is what makes the derivative at the extremum a genuine limit of difference quotients. The equal endpoint values then stop the extreme value from sitting at both ends, so it must sit in the interior, where differentiability turns the local extremum into a zero of the derivative. Weaken any one of them and the conclusion is no longer guaranteed.
questions.hint: Ask where the extreme value theorem may be applied, and where the derivative must exist.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: The Rolle hypothesis that fails at a single point
questions.learningObjective: identify which hypothesis a familiar counterexample to Rolle's theorem breaks
questions.stem: Let f of x be the absolute value of x on the interval from minus 1 to 1. The function is continuous there and takes the value 1 at both endpoints, so the conclusion of Rolle's theorem looks reachable. Which hypothesis does it actually break?

options.text: It fails the requirement that the endpoint values be equal, since the two ends differ in sign
options.misconception: reads the endpoints as the signed values minus 1 and 1 rather than the function values

options.text: It fails the requirement that the interval be closed, since minus 1 and 1 are both excluded
options.misconception: thinks a closed interval must contain the derivative at its endpoints to be usable

options.text: It fails continuity on the closed interval, because the absolute value has a corner there
options.misconception: believes a corner makes a function discontinuous, when the absolute value is continuous everywhere

options.text: It fails differentiability on the open interval, because the derivative does not exist at zero
options.misconception: confuses the failure of the two-sided derivative at a corner with a failure of continuity

questions.explanation: The absolute value is the difference of two linear pieces, so it is continuous everywhere, including at zero, and the endpoint values 1 and 1 are equal. What fails is the derivative: the left slope at zero is minus 1 and the right slope is 1, so no single derivative exists there. Rolle's theorem only needs the derivative in the open interior, and zero is interior, so the missing derivative is exactly the gap. This is why the theorem is stated with differentiability on the open interval rather than everywhere.
questions.hint: Compute the one-sided slopes at zero and see which condition they destroy.

questions.topic: Counting Rolle points for a cubic

questions.stem: Let f of x equal x cubed minus 3x. On the interval from minus 1 to 2 the function takes the value 2 at both endpoints, so Rolle's theorem applies. How many points in that open interval have a zero derivative? Report the count as a whole number.
questions.explanation: Differentiating gives 3x squared minus 3, which vanishes when x squared equals 1, that is at x equal to minus 1 and at x equal to 1. The point minus 1 is an endpoint of the interval, not an interior point, so it is excluded: Rolle's theorem promises a point in the open interval. A dense numeric scan of 3x squared minus 3 over the interior finds exactly one sign change, at x equal to 1, which matches the symbolic solution set. Counting the two algebraic roots without checking the interval is the usual slip here.
questions.hint: Solve the derivative for zero, then throw away any root that is not strictly inside the interval.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Counting Rolle points for a sine curve
questions.learningObjective: count the interior stationary points of a trigonometric function on a given interval
questions.stem: Let f of x equal the sine of 3 pi x. It takes the value 0 at x equal to 0 and again at x equal to two thirds, so Rolle's theorem guarantees at least one stationary point in between. How many stationary points lie in the open interval from 0 to two thirds? Report the count as a whole number.
questions.explanation: The derivative is 3 pi times the cosine of 3 pi x, and it vanishes when 3 pi x equals pi over 2 plus any whole multiple of pi, that is at x equal to one sixth, one half, and then at four thirds, which is past the endpoint. Exactly two of these, one sixth and one half, lie in the open interval from 0 to two thirds. Sampling the cosine on a fine grid and counting sign changes gives the same count of two, which is the independent check that no third crossing hides between the samples.
questions.hint: Set the cosine of 3 pi x equal to zero and list every solution, then test which fall inside the interval.

questions.topic: Endpoint values that block Rolle's theorem
questions.learningObjective: recognise that Rolle's theorem needs equal endpoint values before it can be used
questions.stem: A student wants to apply Rolle's theorem to f of x equal to x cubed minus 3x on the interval from 0 to 2, and notices the derivative does vanish inside. Which observation tells the student the theorem does not apply?

options.text: The function is not differentiable at x equal to 0, so the theorem cannot be used at all
options.misconception: insists on differentiability at the closed endpoints, which the theorem never asks for

options.text: The derivative vanishes only once inside, so the theorem must be applied twice for a full answer
options.misconception: thinks the number of interior stationary points has to match some fixed count

options.text: The function takes the value 0 at 0 and the value 2 at 2, so the endpoint values are unequal
options.misconception: overlooks that the two endpoint values are different, which is the hypothesis that fails

options.text: The interval from 0 to 2 is not closed, so the extreme value theorem cannot be applied
options.misconception: believes the interval 0 to 2 fails to be a closed interval, when both endpoints are included

questions.explanation: Rolle's theorem is built for functions that come back to where they started. Here the function climbs from 0 to 2 across the interval, so the equal endpoint condition fails and nothing forces an extremum into the interior. The theorem gives no information here, and the stationary point at x equal to 1 that the student spotted is a fact about the algebra, not a consequence of Rolle. The general version of the theorem, the mean value theorem, covers intervals whose endpoint values differ.
questions.hint: Evaluate the function at both endpoints of the interval and compare the two values.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Zeros bounded by a count of critical points
questions.learningObjective: use a count of critical points to bound the number of zeros of a function
questions.stem: A function f is continuous on the closed interval from a to b, differentiable on its interior, and its derivative vanishes at exactly one interior point. What is the largest number of zeros f can have strictly inside the interval?

options.text: At most three, because each zero of f forces two extra zeros of the derivative
options.misconception: double counts the Rolle points, adding a spurious zero on each side

options.text: At most two, because each additional zero of f forces an extra zero of the derivative
options.misconception: pairs zeros of the function with zeros of the derivative one for one, so the count is too tight

options.text: No upper bound at all, because a function can cross the axis as often as it likes
options.misconception: ignores Rolle's theorem, thinking oscillations are limited by nothing

options.text: At most one, because every zero of f must also be a zero of its derivative there
options.misconception: believes zeros of a function and zeros of its derivative have to coincide

questions.explanation: Between any two consecutive zeros of f, Rolle's theorem supplies a distinct point where the derivative vanishes. Two zeros of f already force one zero of the derivative between them, and three zeros of f would force two. With only one zero of the derivative available, at most two zeros of f are possible, and the bound is sharp: the function (x minus one half)(x minus three halves) on the interval from 0 to 2 has derivative 2x minus 2, which vanishes exactly once, at x equal to 1, while the function itself has two interior zeros.
questions.hint: Apply Rolle's theorem on the interval between each pair of consecutive zeros of the function.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: A derivative that never vanishes on an interval
questions.learningObjective: explain why a derivative that never vanishes cannot have equal endpoint values
questions.stem: Suppose f is continuous on the closed interval from a to b, differentiable on its interior, and its derivative is never zero at an interior point. If in addition f of a equals f of b, what follows?

options.text: No such function exists, because a zero-free derivative keeps one strict sign throughout
options.misconception: misses that a derivative with no zeros cannot change sign without passing through zero

options.text: f must also be differentiable at the two endpoints, since the interval has been closed up
options.misconception: believes the interior hypotheses force differentiability at the closed endpoints

options.text: f must be constant on the whole interval, since a zero-free derivative gives no change at all
options.misconception: jumps from a derivative that never vanishes straight to the claim of a constant function

options.text: f must attain an absolute extremum strictly inside the interval, as Rolle's theorem requires
options.misconception: applies Rolle's theorem although the equal endpoint values do force an interior extremum here

questions.explanation: A derivative cannot change sign without passing through zero, because derivatives have the intermediate value property. So a derivative that is never zero on the whole interior is either always positive or always negative there, and the mean value theorem then makes f strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on the interval. Either way the endpoint values must differ, contradicting the assumption that they are equal. The described function therefore cannot exist, which is a quick proof that a zero-free derivative is incompatible with a return to the starting value.
questions.hint: Ask whether a derivative can change sign without taking the value zero, then use the mean value theorem.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: A repeated root of a polynomial
questions.learningObjective: interpret a repeated root of a polynomial in terms of the derivative
questions.stem: A polynomial p of degree 3 has a repeated root at x equal to 2, so the value of p at 2 is 0 and the value of the derivative of p at 2 is also 0. What does that say about the graph of p and the horizontal line y equals 0?

options.text: The graph meets the line at x equal to 2 and continues with the same slope on both sides
options.misconception: confuses the derivative being zero with the slope being unchanged across the point

options.text: The graph crosses the line at x equal to 2, and the crossing is a simple one with the usual slope
options.misconception: assumes a zero of the polynomial is automatically a simple crossing of the axis

options.text: The graph stays entirely above the line for all x, so the root cannot be visible at all
options.misconception: reads a zero of a polynomial as meaning the function is never actually equal to zero

options.text: The graph meets the line at x equal to 2 and turns back, touching without crossing there
options.misconception: believes a flat point of a polynomial must lie below the axis rather than on it

questions.explanation: A root of multiplicity two, or higher, leaves the derivative zero at the root itself, so the tangent line there is the horizontal axis itself. The curve is therefore flat at the point of contact and lies on one side of the axis on both sides, which is a touch rather than a crossing. The only way for a smooth curve to cross the axis is to change sign there, and a sign change at a differentiable point forces a nonzero derivative. Cubics with a repeated root factor as a product of a linear factor taken twice, which is the algebraic statement of the same fact.
questions.hint: Ask what a horizontal tangent at a point where the function is zero does to the graph locally.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Proof structure of Rolle's theorem
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of the standard proof of Rolle's theorem
questions.stem: Put these four moves in the order that turns the hypotheses of Rolle's theorem into its conclusion about the derivative.

options.text: Continuity on the closed interval lets the extreme value theorem produce an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on it
Equal endpoint values forbid the extreme value from being taken at both ends at once
One of the two extreme values is therefore attained strictly inside the interval, at some point c
Differentiability at that interior point forces the derivative there to equal zero

questions.explanation: The proof chains the three hypotheses in a fixed order. The extreme value theorem first needs continuity on the closed interval, and it hands back an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum that are attained. The second hypothesis, equal endpoint values, then rules out the possibility that the same value is taken at both endpoints, because then both extremes could sit at the ends. At least one extreme must therefore be interior, at some point c, where the third hypothesis applies: at an interior local extremum of a differentiable function the derivative is zero. Skipping the middle step is what makes students think the theorem needs no endpoint condition at all.
questions.hint: Each hypothesis is used exactly once, and the last one is applied at the point the earlier steps produce.

questions.topic: Mean value theorem against Rolle's theorem
questions.learningObjective: state how the mean value theorem generalises Rolle's theorem
questions.stem: The mean value theorem is often described as a generalisation of Rolle's theorem. Which statement describes the relationship between the two correctly?

options.misconception: thinks continuity must hold in the interior and not on the closed interval

options.text: The mean value theorem is a separate result with no relationship to Rolle's theorem at all
options.misconception: treats the two theorems as unrelated because the endpoint condition looks different

options.text: The mean value theorem drops the equal endpoint condition and concludes the derivative equals an average rate of change
The mean value theorem keeps the equal endpoint condition and weakens the conclusion to a sign statement
options.misconception: keeps the endpoint restriction and thinks only the conclusion is relaxed

questions.topic: Average rate of change from endpoint values
questions.learningObjective: compute the average rate of change that the mean value theorem forces the derivative to attain
questions.stem: A function f rises from the value 5 at x equal to 2 to the value 21 at x equal to 6. The mean value theorem says that at some point c strictly between 2 and 6 the derivative equals the average rate of change across the interval. What is that value of the derivative?
questions.explanation: The average rate of change is the change in the function divided by the change in the input, here (21 minus 5) divided by (6 minus 2), that is 16 over 4, which is 4. The theorem guarantees that the instantaneous rate hits this average somewhere strictly inside the interval, even though the rate may be much larger or smaller at other points. The direction of the difference matters: with the bounds written in the order 6 then 2 both numerator and denominator change sign, so the average is unchanged.
questions.hint: Divide the change in the function value by the change in x, then simplify the fraction.

Substituting back, 3c squared is 13 to machine precision, so the derivative there does equal the average rate.

The derivative of the square root of x is 1 over 2 times the square root of x, and setting that equal to one third gives the square root of c equal to 3 over 2, so c equals 9 over 4, which is 2.25. The theorem needs continuity only on the closed interval and differentiability only inside, so the fact that the derivative blows up as x approaches zero causes no problem here, since zero is not in the interval. questions.topic: Discontinuity at an endpoint of a mean value interval
questions.learningObjective: see how a jump at a closed endpoint defeats the mean value conclusion
questions.stem: Define f of x as the square root of x for x greater than 0, and set f of 0 equal to 5. A student claims the mean value theorem on the interval from 0 to 1 gives a point c where the derivative equals the average rate. Why is there no such point?

options.text: The derivative has no value at zero, so the theorem cannot be applied on an interval containing it
options.misconception: thinks differentiability is required at the closed endpoints of the interval

options.text: The function is not continuous at zero, since 5 is not the limit of the square root there
options.misconception: describes the discontinuity accurately but claims the theorem needs continuity in the open interior

options.text: The average rate is minus 4, and the derivative is positive throughout, so no point can have a negative value of it
options.misconception: ignores that the required slope is negative while every available derivative is positive

options.text: The average rate is 4, and the derivative of the square root is never that large on the interval
options.misconception: gets the sign of the average rate wrong by subtracting in the wrong order

The consequences confirm this: the average rate of change is (1 minus 5) divided by 1, that is minus 4, while the derivative 1 over 2 times the square root of x is positive for every interior point, so the required slope simply is not attained.

questions.learningObjective: use a derivative ceiling below one to prove a fixed point equation has exactly one solution
questions.stem: Let f of x equal the cosine of x. On the interval from 0 to 1 the magnitude of its derivative never exceeds 0.8415, and the function maps that interval into itself. questions.explanation: Existence and uniqueness come from two different tools. For existence, the function g of x equal to the cosine of x minus x is continuous on the interval, and it is positive at 0 and negative at 1, since the cosine of 1 is 0.540302, so the intermediate value theorem gives a solution inside. For uniqueness, the mean value theorem says that two solutions r and s would satisfy the magnitude of r minus s equal to the magnitude of the cosine of r minus the cosine of s, which is at most 0.8415 times the magnitude of r minus s, and that forces r to equal s. questions.hint: Use the intermediate value theorem for existence, then the mean value theorem to rule out a second solution.

questions.topic: Conditions of Cauchy's mean value theorem
questions.learningObjective: state the hypotheses of Cauchy's mean value theorem
questions.stem: Cauchy's mean value theorem compares the rates of change of two functions on one interval. Which pair of conditions is what it actually assumes?

options.text: Both are continuous in the interior of the interval, and both derivatives exist at every interior point
options.misconception: leaks continuity out of the closed interval, where the extreme value step needs it

options.text: Both are differentiable on the closed interval, and the first derivative never vanishes
options.misconception: asks for differentiability at the endpoints and puts the nonvanishing on the wrong function

options.text: Both are continuous on the closed interval, and the second function is strictly increasing throughout
options.misconception: treats a strictly increasing second function as if it guaranteed a nonzero derivative

options.text: Both are continuous on the closed interval, both differentiable in the interior, and the second derivative never vanishes

questions.explanation: Cauchy's theorem carries the same two regularity conditions as the ordinary mean value theorem, applied to both functions at once, and adds one extra condition: the derivative of the denominator function must not vanish in the interior, since the conclusion divides by it. Strict increase is not enough, because a function can climb steadily while its derivative passes through zero, for instance a cubic on a short interval. options.text: The function is increasing on that interval, and no concavity statement follows

questions.explanation: Between any two points of the interval the mean value theorem produces an interior point where the derivative equals the average rate of change, and here that derivative is positive, so the average rate of change is positive and the function is increasing. Curvature is a separate question, settled by the sign of the second derivative, and nothing in the sign of the first derivative constrains it. The extreme value theorem has no role here at all, which is why the conclusion is about ordering rather than about a maximum.
questions.hint: Apply the mean value theorem to two points of the interval and read off the sign of the difference of values.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Vertical gap between a curve and its tangent
questions.learningObjective: measure how far a convex curve sits above its tangent line
questions.stem: For the curve with height f of x equal to x cubed, the tangent line at x equal to 1 has height 1 plus 3 times the quantity x minus 1. At x equal to 3, what is the vertical distance from that line up to the curve?
questions.explanation: The curve stands at 27 when x equal to 3, and the tangent line stands at 1 plus 3 times 2, that is 7. The vertical distance between them is 27 minus 7, that is 20. The direction of the gap matters: a function whose second derivative is positive everywhere is convex, and a convex curve lies above its tangent lines everywhere, so the curve sits higher rather than lower. The same computation at x equal to 0 gives a distance of 2, since the curve stands at 0 there while the line stands at minus 2, which confirms that the curve stays above the line on both sides of the point of tangency.
questions.hint: Evaluate the curve and the tangent line at x equal to 3 and subtract the lower from the higher.

questions.topic: Chord below a concave curve

questions.stem: The curve with height f of x equal to the square root of x is concave for positive x, so the straight line joining the points (0, 0) and (4, 2) lies below it. At x equal to 1, what is the vertical distance from that line up to the curve?
questions.explanation: The line through those two points has height x divided by 2, so at x equal to 1 its height is 0.5, while the curve there stands at 1. The vertical distance from the line up to the curve is 1 minus 0.5, that is 0.5. Concavity is the reason the chord lies below: the second derivative of the square root of x is minus 1 over 4 x to the three halves, which is negative, so the curve is bowed downward and every chord stays under it. The same computation at x equal to 3 gives 1.5 minus the square root of 3, so the gap narrows as the endpoint is approached.
questions.hint: The line has height x over 2, so evaluate both heights at x equal to 1 and subtract.

questions.topic: Sign of the gap for a concave function
questions.learningObjective: predict whether a tangent line sits above or below a concave curve
questions.stem: A function is concave on an interval, meaning its second derivative is negative there. How does the tangent line at any point of that interval sit relative to the curve?

options.misconception: invents extra crossings from the size of the second derivative rather than its sign

options.text: The tangent line and the curve coincide wherever the derivative is zero
options.misconception: believes a zero derivative makes a whole line coincide with a curve

options.text: The tangent line is on or above the curve everywhere on the interval
The tangent line is on or below the curve everywhere on the interval
options.misconception: reverses the tangent and chord inequalities that go with a negative second derivative

questions.explanation: For a concave function the derivative is decreasing, so as the input moves away from the point of tangency the slope of the curve falls below the slope of the tangent on one side and the curve ends up under the line, while on the other side the curve falls more slowly and stays under the line too. The tangent line is therefore a support line from above at every point. The chord inequality points the other way: for a concave function the chord lies below the curve, which is the pairing that makes the trapezoid rule underestimate.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Tangent line as an upper bound for a concave model
questions.learningObjective: use concavity to turn a model into a bound on its future values
questions.stem: A population model P is concave for all t at least 0, with P of 0 equal to 200 and the derivative of P at 0 equal to 60. Explain why the model can never exceed the line with height 200 plus 60 t for t at least 0.

answer.exemplar: A concave function lies below its tangent line at every point, and the tangent line at t equal to 0 has height 200 plus 60 t, so P of t is at most 200 plus 60 t for every t at least 0.

questions.explanation: The line 200 plus 60 t is exactly the tangent line to P at the point where the model has value 200 and rate 60, because a tangent line is the value at the point plus the slope times the distance from the point. Concavity says the tangent line lies above the curve, so the line is an upper bound on the model at every later time. A concave growth curve therefore starts at 200 and can never grow faster on average than its initial rate, which is the practical content of the statement. The bound is not attained except at t equal to 0, where the two coincide.
questions.hint: Identify the line as the tangent line to the model at t equal to 0, then use the tangent and chord inequalities for a concave function.

options.text: Only at x equal to 0, where the curve meets its own tangent line
Only at x equal to 1, where the curve has grown by a factor of e

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Where a proof by the mean value theorem fails
questions.learningObjective: identify the error in a misapplied mean value theorem argument
questions.stem: A student writes: the mean value theorem gives a point in every interval where the derivative equals the average rate of change, so the derivative must be constant on any closed interval. What is wrong with the argument?

options.text: The theorem pins the derivative down at one interior point, not at every point of the interval
options.misconception: turns the existence of a single interior point into a claim about all points

options.text: The theorem needs equal endpoint values, so it does not apply to most functions at all
options.misconception: confuses the mean value theorem with Rolle's theorem, which does need them

options.text: The theorem only applies to polynomials, so curved functions are left out of it
options.misconception: believes the theorem is restricted to polynomial functions

options.text: Nothing is wrong with the conclusion, since the average rate fixes the derivative at every point
options.misconception: accepts a constant-derivative conclusion from an existence statement

questions.explanation: The theorem is an existence statement: for one chosen pair of endpoints it produces one interior point, and it says nothing about the derivative at any other point of the interval. A function such as the square of x on the interval from 1 to 3 is the clean counterexample, since the average rate is 4 and the derivative equals 4 at exactly one interior point, while the derivative takes every value from 2 to 6 elsewhere on the interval. The endpoint hypothesis in the student's statement is a confusion with Rolle's theorem, which is the special case where the average rate is zero.
questions.hint: Test the claim on the square of x over an interval where the derivative is obviously not constant.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Continuity of the derivative is not required
questions.learningObjective: state which regularity the mean value theorem actually demands
questions.stem: Does the mean value theorem require the derivative of the function to be continuous inside the interval?

options.text: Yes, because the proof passes a limit through the derivative, so the derivative must be continuous
options.misconception: believes the proof needs the derivative to be a continuous function

options.text: Yes, but the requirement is waived when the derivative is discontinuous at the two endpoints
options.misconception: moves the continuity requirement to the endpoints, which are never covered anyway

options.text: No, but only because a derivative can never be discontinuous on an interval
options.misconception: rejects the right answer for the wrong reason, denying the standard example

options.text: No, continuity of the function on the closed interval and differentiability inside are enough

questions.explanation: The proof of the mean value theorem applies Rolle's theorem to a difference between the function and its secant line, and Rolle's theorem needs only continuity on the closed interval and differentiability in the interior. A derivative may be discontinuous, and the standard example of the square of x times the sine of 1 over x, defined to be 0 at zero, has a derivative that exists everywhere while oscillating without limit near zero. The theorem still applies to such a function, which is why differentiability of f and continuity of the derivative of f are kept as separate conditions in a first course.
questions.hint: Look at the hypotheses of Rolle's theorem, since the mean value theorem is proved by applying it to a secant difference.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Instantaneous rate equal to the average
questions.learningObjective: identify the instant at which a measured rate equals the average rate
questions.stem: A tank's liquid level rises 1.8 metres in 6 hours. The mean value theorem guarantees an instant at which the rate of rise equalled the average over those 6 hours. What was that rate?

options.text: 10.8 metres per hour, from multiplying the rise by the elapsed time
options.misconception: multiplies the two quantities instead of dividing, inverting the average rate

options.text: 2.1 metres per hour, from adding the total rise to the average rate
options.misconception: adds a total and a rate together, mixing two different kinds of quantity

options.text: 0.3 metres per hour, the average rate over the whole interval
0.3 metres, the total rise rather than a rate of change
options.misconception: reports a total change where a rate per unit time was asked for

questions.explanation: An average rate of change is a change divided by the time it took, so 1.8 metres over 6 hours is 1.8 divided by 6, that is 0.3 metres per hour. The mean value theorem then guarantees that at some instant inside those 6 hours the instantaneous rate of rise was exactly that value, whatever the rate did at other moments. The dimension is worth checking: dividing a length by a time gives a length per time, which is what a rate must be, and multiplying instead would give 10.8 metres hours per hour, which is not a rate at all.
questions.hint: Divide the change in level by the time taken, and check that the units come out as a rate.

questions.topic: Instantaneous rate read off an exponential model
questions.learningObjective: extract a growth constant from a doubling over a stated interval
questions.stem: A colony of bacteria is modelled by 1200 times the exponential of k t, with t in years, and it doubles from 1200 to 2400 in 6 years. What is the value of k? Report your answer to six decimal places.
questions.explanation: Doubling means that 1200 times the exponential of 6k equals 2400, so the exponential of 6k equals 2 and taking the natural logarithm gives 6k equal to the natural logarithm of 2, that is k equal to the natural logarithm of 2 over 6, which is 0.115525 to six decimal places. The mean value theorem ties this to the rate: the model grows from 1200 to 2400 in 6 years, an average of 200 per year, and the instantaneous rate reaches 200 at the moment when 1200 times k times the exponential of kt equals 200, which is a check on the same constant rather than a second value of it.

questions.topic: Bound from a ceiling on the derivative

questions.stem: A function has the values 3, 7, 15 and 31 at the inputs 1, 2, 3 and 4, and the magnitude of its derivative never exceeds 5 anywhere on the interval from 1 to 4. What is the largest change in the function that the mean value theorem can guarantee between the inputs 1 and 4?
questions.explanation: The ceiling of 5 over an interval of length 3 bounds the change by 5 times 3, that is 15. The tabulated values show why a bound is not an estimate: the actual change from 3 to 31 is 28, which is larger than 15, and the two are consistent precisely because the ceiling is a worst case over the whole interval while the function here grows faster than 5 per unit in places. The ceiling is the only information the theorem can use, so 15 is the largest change it can guarantee, not the change that occurs.
questions.hint: Multiply the ceiling by the length of the interval, which is 4 minus 1.

questions.topic: Critical points forced by a zero count
questions.learningObjective: use Rolle's theorem repeatedly to force a number of stationary points
questions.stem: A continuous function has four distinct zeros inside an interval. Applying Rolle's theorem repeatedly, what is the smallest number of zeros of its derivative inside that same interval?

options.text: None, because a function can cross the axis repeatedly with a derivative that never vanishes
options.misconception: believes a function may cross the axis many times without any stationary point between

options.text: Three, one between each consecutive pair of zeros of the function
Five, counting one extra beyond each gap as well as the gaps themselves
options.misconception: adds an extra stationary point at each end that Rolle's theorem never supplies

options.misconception: counts the gaps between zeros without pairing each gap with a zero of the derivative

The theorem can only be applied between two points where the function is zero, never at a crossing itself.
questions.hint: Count the gaps between consecutive zeros and apply Rolle's theorem once in each gap.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Why no formula for the mean value point
questions.learningObjective: explain why the mean value theorem gives existence rather than a location
questions.stem: Explain why the mean value theorem does not supply a formula that computes the point c where the derivative equals the average rate of change.

answer.exemplar: The theorem is proved by applying the extreme value theorem to a difference between the function and its secant line, and that argument only asserts that an extremum exists; it never identifies where, and the point depends on the whole shape of the graph rather than on the endpoint values alone.

questions.explanation: The proof locates the point indirectly: it takes a secant line, forms the difference from the function, and shows that the difference attains an extreme value somewhere in the interior, where the derivative must be zero. Nothing in that argument singles out a location, so the theorem is an existence statement and nothing more. Students who want the actual point must solve the equation that the derivative equals the average rate, and that equation can be as hard as the original problem, which is exactly why a numerical search for the point is often the practical route.
questions.hint: Recall which existence theorem the proof is built on, and ask whether it reports a location.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Existence without a unique location
questions.learningObjective: interpret a theorem that guarantees a point without saying which one
questions.stem: A theorem guarantees that at least one point in an open interval has a stated property, and a graph shows three such points. What follows about the theorem's conclusion?

options.text: The conclusion holds, since a guarantee of at least one point is satisfied by three of them
The conclusion fails, because the theorem named one point and the graph names three
options.misconception: reads an existence claim as a claim that the point is unique

options.text: The conclusion holds only if the three points all give the same value of the function
options.misconception: adds an equality of function values that the theorem never asked for

options.text: The conclusion is undecidable, since a graph cannot be trusted to locate the points
options.misconception: treats a reading from a graph as inherently unusable

questions.explanation: The language of the theorem is at least one, so any configuration containing one qualifying point satisfies it, and three is more than enough. What the theorem does not deliver is uniqueness, and a proof that needs the unique point must argue separately that no other point qualifies, usually by counting sign changes or by showing the derivative has a fixed sign. The value of such a statement is that it converts a picture into a fact: the graph suggested the property and the theorem makes it independent of how carefully the graph was drawn.
questions.hint: Read the quantifier in the statement of the theorem before judging the graph.
